tldr: TornadoVM's library tasks let Java code mix its own GPU kernels with NVIDIA's cuFFT, cuBLAS, cuDNN and cuDF in one task graph, without JNI, Python or C++.
summary: Java runs the enterprise, but NVIDIA's tuned libraries (cuBLAS, cuFFT, cuDNN, CUTLASS, cuDF, cuVS) are normally reached through a Python sidecar, JNI or FFM bindings, or a C++ rewrite. TornadoVM runs on any JDK 21+, compiles Java to OpenCL, CUDA PTX or Metal, and offers four levels: the @Parallel loop annotation, the low-level KernelContext API, a new TileContext API mirroring NVIDIA's tile model, and library tasks. A library task calls a function such as cuFFT's R2C forward transform, named and parameterised as in NVIDIA's docs, on FFM-backed data. It chains in a task graph with Java-written kernels, so data stays on the GPU.

Demos showed a low-pass filter built from cuFFT plus custom Java kernels, and a matrix-multiplication comparison profiled with Nsight Systems, where hand-tuned KernelContext and TileContext kernels reached about 90% of cuBLAS. The team's Java LLM inference engine reached 90-95% of llama.cpp throughput on Gemma and Qwen models, after being about 30x slower a year earlier. Mary Xekalaki offloaded Apache Flink SQL, via a config flag, to cuDF Parquet reading, cuDF string matching and a JIT kernel: up to 17x faster on 64 million rows than one Flink slot. They also reported 90x faster JVector graph builds with Cassandra.
keyPoints: TornadoVM ships as JARs on Maven Central and SDKs via SDKMAN, and runs on OpenJDK, GraalVM, Temurin, Zulu and other JDK 21+ builds.
Library tasks are named so the runtime can optimise data movement across a task graph. Runtime features such as CUDA graphs, multiple streams and grid scheduling cut transfer overhead.
TileContext moves thread, prefetch and cache decisions to NVIDIA's compiler and is much more compact than equivalent KernelContext code using tensor-core MMA fragments.
Profiling combines JFR for the JVM side with NVIDIA Nsight for the GPU timeline, plus TornadoVM's own tools.
The Flink integration analyses the query IR and maps operations to library tasks where possible and JIT tasks otherwise, with no change to the SQL.
The speakers reported that TornadoVM's generated kernels now reach 98% of the kernel time of equivalent hand-written CUDA, and that the LLM engine beats llama.cpp prefill by 12% in some cases.
takeaways: Install TornadoVM via SDKMAN and run a first kernel on your laptop GPU before targeting NVIDIA servers.
Use library tasks for operations NVIDIA already optimises (GEMM, FFT, Parquet decode), and write only the glue steps as Java kernels.
Profile with JFR together with Nsight Systems to see where data transfers, not compute, dominate.

quotes.text: We have reached a point that Java can access the GPU like any other native.

watchIf: You want GPU acceleration or NVIDIA libraries in a Java application without JNI, Python or C++, and want to see actual performance numbers.
